entry.dc:title: Environmental problems of coal production in the federal republic of of germany with particular reference to to the Ruhr
entry.dc:creator: Petsch G.
entry.dc:description: In 1979 it was noted that the production of deep-mined coal in the Federal Republic of Germany, including the Ruhr area, has risen once again. Since the beginning of the sixties the convenient source of both energy and raw material, oil, has been responsible for the falling levels of coal production in the Ruhr, to almost one half of peak production in 1956. Not much would have been needed to give up the entire troublesome and expensive process of deep coal mining in the Federal Republic in favour of the then cheap and bountiful oil. Only lignite managed to maintain a more or less steady annual production rate due to the direct conversion into electricity of a major part of its production at the site of extraction. Since the limitations and uncertainties governing the supply of crude oil have now been clearly exposed, the illusions about oil have begun to fade, and as a result confidence in our indigenous supplies of energy and raw material resources has been restored. What, however, are the implications of this revival of home-produced energy and raw material, which are not without problems both when produced and when consumed for the region in which they are extracted and brought to the surface, and where, to a large extent, the processing takes place? The region benefits from employment and investment, and in turn offers its resources (labour, land, water, air) inasmuch as past development has left them available for future development. But is the region to be covered with even more 'honourable' scars? In 1980, 87 million tonnes of deep mined coal were produced in the Federal Republic of Germany which resulted in roughly the same amount of minestone (spoil). Approximately 600 km<sup>2</sup> of densely populated area in the Ruhr district was already acquiring artificial drainage due to subsidence. Coking plants and old coal-based stations fired with deep mined coal pollute air and water. Lignite production in 1980 in the Federal Republic of Germany - which was almost entirely obtained by opencast mining - amounted to 130 million tonnes. To achieve this an additional 445×10<sup>6</sup>m<sup>3</sup> of overburden had to be shifted. Already in 1977 in the Rhineland between Cologne, Dusseldorf and Aachen (Aix-la-Chapelle), 522 km<sup>2</sup> of mainly good agricultural land was acquired under compulsory purchase order for lignite mining. Villages, roads, rail and waterways were and continue to be re-routed and re-sited. The direct conversion of lignite into electricity produces emission and spreads pollution. Now, it is not only the people of the Ruhr area, the largest industrial conurbation in Europe, that have become sensitive to the impact of mining upon their environment. In all industrial countries it has been learned that those things which cannot be replaced, i.e. environment, are not always being valued by the free market at a price which represents the value they may have for the individual and possibly should have for all of us. Today the need for mining is hardly being questioned any more but people are voicing their opinion as to what is a just price to be paid. The citizen of the Ruhr, for instance, no longer accepts that the specific environmental impacts caused by deep coal mining, which produces a commodity wanted by the entire nation, should be borne solely at the place where it is produced and by the people who happen to live there. He demands that such burdens are borne by everybody who enjoys the benefits. Clear political ideas must be developed and made know as to how much we value home-produced energy sources, what proportion of the resulting burdens the country is willing to bear and how they are to be distributed fairly. There are many methods and technical means by which the burdens of the mining and industrial regions can be minimised, by which damage can be repaired and derelict areas reclaimed. The application of such means must be safeguarded by early planning and sufficient finanacing so that the exploitation of one resource will not result in other resources being lost. © 1982 Science and Technology Letters.

entry.dc:title: The design of a microprocessor-based instrument for the seismic interrogation of rock masses
entry.dc:creator: Hill J.J.
entry.dc:description: This paper describes a microcomputer-based instrument which is used for the recording and spectral processing of seismic signals obtained in opencast mining. Various types of vector attenuation spectra can be computed and displayed. The instrument is used to evaluate indirectly the brokenness of rock masses prior to blasting. © 1982.

entry.dc:title: Effects of stockpiling topsoils associated with opencast mining 1. Chemical properties and the growth of ryegrass and white clover.
entry.dc:creator: Widdowson J.
entry.dc:description: Two stockpiles were studied: one at Mataura, formed from Mataura silt loam (recent soil), was associated with opencast lignite mining; the other at Lorneville near Invercargill, formed mainly from Makarewa silt loam (gleyed recent soil), was associated with opencast mining of ceramic clays. Ryegrass yields in soils from the top of the stockpiles were similar to those in unstored topsoil from under pasture. Yields from the lower part of the stockpile were higher than those at the surface because of high levels of mineral N that had accumulated under anaerobic conditions. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: Land drainage and restoration of land after NCB opencast mining ( UK).
entry.dc:creator: Bragg N.
entry.dc:description: So far the work has been aimed at identifying the problems of reinstated soils and how these affect drainage design. The physical soil examinations have indicated that the soils on reinstated sites are very different from their undisturbed neighbours. The monitoring of drainage on sites of differing age from reinstatement indicates that where a true control is established there are significant differences between the worked and unworked land. -Author

entry.dc:title: Effects of stockpiling topsoils associated with opencast mining 2. Physical properties.
entry.dc:creator: McQueen D.J.
entry.dc:description: Physical properties of 2 topsoil stockpiles associated with opencast mining were studied in the Mataura and Lorneville areas, Southland. In both cases, stockpiling resulted in increased bulk density and mechanical strength and decreased porosity, especially macroporosity. These changes are attributed to the influence of earthmoving equipment rather than the 'overburden' effect of stockpiling. The major effect of stockpiling on soil physical conditions appears to be soil compaction which occurs during formation of the pile. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: TECHNO-ECONOMIC FEASIBILITY OF OPENCAST MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Jinarajan G.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: Some technological, operational and economic aspects of opencast coal mining are considered with special reference to the conditions prevailing in Indian mines. It is shown that purely viewing from a technical angle the scope for opencast mining is vast but each project requires a thorough economic analysis.

entry.dc:title: DEVELOPMENT OF RESPONSE SPECTRA TECHNIQUES FOR PREDICTION OF STRUCTURAL DAMAGE FROM OPEN-PIT BLASTING VIBRATIONS.
entry.dc:creator: Walker S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the Institution of Mining and Metallurgy Section A Mining Technology
entry.dc:description: Structural damage from blasting vibrations has been a major problem associated with opencast mining and quarrying operations for many years. Investigations have shown that there are many inadequacies in the conventional method that is used to limit the amounts of explosive and distances to local buildings. A more rational method of predicting damage is based on response spectra techniques, which were originally developed in the field of earthquake engineering. These techniques have been adapted for use in opencast mining and the results of the research to date show that the conventional methods, based on peak particle velocity measurements, can result in overrestrictive site blasting practices.

entry.dc:title: COMBINED MINING SYSTEMS FOR OPEN PIT MINES.
entry.dc:creator: Franke R.
entry.dc:description: Production rates in opencast mines will have to be increased in the future, especially in the energy sector. Reactions for this development are an increased demand for coal, oil-sand and oil-shale, the steadily growing share of opencast mining operations as opposed to a decreasing share for underground mining, and the increase of the overburden-to-pay mineral ratio. Various possible combined opencast mining systems are presented and explained by practical examples.

entry.dc:title: Coal and the environment.
entry.dc:description: Produced by the Commission on Energy and the Environment, contains the following chapters: the coal industry: decline and renaissance; prospects for coal; framework of environmental control; deep mining; subsidence; spoil: dereliction and pit closures; opencast mining; coal markets; transport, handling and storage; conversion to substitute fuels; combustion technology; combustion residues; sources, quantities, control and effects; environmental effects of burning coal in urban areas; and the planning process reconciling the interests.-from CEGB Digest

entry.dc:title: Shifts in US coal production: trends and implications.
entry.dc:creator: Davis J.
entry.dc:description: In the last 20 yr coal's importance has revived. The distribution of resources is described with particular reference to greater emphasis on opencast mining, the new significance of low sulphur coals, and increased production W of the Mississippi. Employment has increased as output revived, but not in proportion to the extra output because of gains in productivity. Massive mining developments have had an environmental impact which has stimulated much conservation activity. Changes in location of production and the nature of the market means that coal tends to move by rail or water, or sometimes by rail/water combined. Transport issues are therefore important. The future of coal in the USA seems assured. -D.G.Price

entry.dc:title: Trends in Opencast Mining at Increased Diesel Prices.
entry.dc:creator: Kutschera S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Erzmetall Journal for Exploration Mining and Metallurgy
entry.dc:description: Cost comparisons between conventional truck haulage and systems consisting of small truck fleets, semi-mobile crushers and belt conveyors show lower operating costs for the latter. Pipeline transport using semi-mobile crushers and semi-mobile mills for grain size reduction could be another solution. Lurgi centrifugal mills, characterized by high capacity, very small dimensions and low capital cost, represent an alternative. German open-pit technology with bucket wheel excavators, shiftable belt conveyors and spreaders operating in conjunction with draglines could be the answer for large strip mines.

entry.dc:title: Environmental impact of iron ore mining and control
entry.dc:creator: Jain N.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: The pollution due to opencast mining in general and iron ore mining in particular is dealt with under the following headings: Air pollution; Water pollution; Noise; Vibrations; Visual intrusions. Suggestions about pollution control measures are given.

entry.dc:title: EXTRACTION OF PILLARS IN THICK COAL SEAMS DEVELOPED IN MULTI-SECTIONS.
entry.dc:creator: Kejriwal B.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: This paper presents a critical review of the current mining practices and the available technological solutions for extracting thick coal seams developed in multi-sections. The methods considered include opencast mining; hydraulic mining; extraction by multi-slice longwall with or without sublevel caving; total underwinning (integral caving) by one slice longwall; and, sublevel caving from galleries.

entry.dc:title: PRECLASSIFYING with Mobile Screen Units in Mobile Crushing Plants.
entry.dc:creator: Sieburg S.
entry.dc:description: Preclassification is becoming an ever-growing necessity in opencast mining systems to meet demands with regard to the end product and output. Optimum economy in crushing and screening plants is first brought about by mobility for which, according to the application, crawler mountings, independent transport crawlers, raft-type walking mechanisms, wheel mountings or rail mountings are employed. The authors present in two examples, with conveying capacities of 2000 and 2800 t. p. h. , two preclassifying screens (circular and linear vibrating screens) in mobile units.

entry.dc:title: DEVELOPMENTS IN MINING CABLES.
entry.dc:creator: Brown R.
entry.dc:description: MEPR (Medium Ethylenepropylene Rubber) was developed for trailing cable use. The characteristics of this compound are given. The electrical properties at high voltages have been proven in opencast mining, where mechanical robustness is a requirement.

entry.dc:title: OPTIMUM - SECOND DRAGLINE ON ITS WAY.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.prism:publicationName: South African Mining and Engineering Journal
entry.dc:description: Gencor's Optimum Colliery, near Hendrina in the Eastern Transvaal is erecting a second dragline. The company intends to concentrate entirely on opencast mining.

entry.dc:title: OPENCAST MINING OPERATIONS IN CUMBRIA.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Since 1958 five sites have been work out and restored for agricultural usage, and four sites are currently in production. Two more sites will be coaling by the end of 1981.

entry.dc:title: Opencast Coal Mining.
entry.dc:creator: Chapier G.
entry.dc:description: This paper briefly reviews the history of France's opencast coal mines ad analyzes various aspects of the opencast mining method. Special emphasis is placed on the comparatively low cost of opencast mining operation. Finally, details are given of the opencast mining practice at the Houilleres de la Loire with particular reference to the thorough and careful land reclamation conducted by this French coal producer at nine mine sites since 1969.

entry.dc:title: The agricultural impact of opencast coal mining in England and Wales
entry.dc:creator: Tomlinson P.
entry.dc:description: Opencast coal mining in England and Wales can cause a wide range of environmental problems which are increasingly public issues due to the planned expansion in output and the impact this may have on agriculture and landscape. Opencast mining is reviewed on a county by county basis to identify the variations in the disturbance caused. A detailed review of restoration techniques and the agricultural quality of the restored land is presented, and the role of Planning Authorities is discussed. Significant variations in the impact of opencast operations are identified, especially in relation to the potential for derelict land reclamation and the grade of agricultural land affected. The latter is generally lower grade 3 and below, although in certain areas operations are entering land of higher agricultural and scenic quality. The quality of restoration, while good, still has scope for improvements, such as reducing soil compaction and the subsequent management of the land by the farmer. The impact on agricultural productivity is difficult to assess, but it appears to be only slight in those cases where recent restoration techniques were used and when lower grade agricultural land is taken. © 1979 Science and Technology Letters.

entry.dc:title: Opencast mining and landscaping
entry.dc:creator: Niemann-Delius C.
entry.dc:description: This paper covers the influence on the environment through opencast mining operations. The effect on the natural surroundings, which still exist when the mine is closed down, is dealt with in particular. Described in this context are the methods of landscaping and the possibilities and criteria for the selection of subsequent applications for the area, which is shown by means of examples.

entry.dc:title: Gosselies 1 Opencast Coal Mine.
entry.dc:creator: Frenay C.
entry.dc:description: For many years in Great Britain and in France relatively shallow deposits of coal - either massive or consisting of a series of seams - have been worked by opencast methods. With this method in mind, a reassessment has been carried out of the carboniferous strata in the Belgian province of Hainaut, in which the coal seams crop out at certain places or are covered by a small thickness of overburden. In October 1980, work was started at a first site at Gosselies and Thimeon (now Charleroi and Pont-a-Celles) at the point where the E 41 and A 54 highways intersect. This site, known as ″Gosselies 1″ , covers an area of 45 hectares and will be worked at depths not exceeding 30 meters. The authors describe the opencast mining method employed and the mining operations which are scheduled to last approximately 28 months.

entry.dc:title: OPENCAST MINING OF BROWN COAL IN EASTERN EUROPE.
entry.dc:creator: Chugh Y.
entry.dc:description: A European technique using bucketwheel excavators, bucket chain excavators, and mobile conveyors bridges may be an alternative for the large lignite mines planned in North Dakota and Texas.

entry.dc:title: MINING THICK COAL SEAMS IN THE SOCIALIST REPUBLIC OF ROMANIA.
entry.dc:creator: Covaci S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: In accordance with the plan for the development of the coal industry, Romania's coal production will exceed 37 million tons by 1980. In the Romanian Socialist Republic, both low grade coals and lignite required as fuel for the energy industry, and high-quality bituminous coal for the iron and steel industry, are mined. The main coal basins bearing thick seams are Oltenia for lignite and the Jiu Valley for bituminous coal. In the Oltenia coal field exploitation is undertaken both by opencast mining in the Rovinari-Jilt region and by underground methods in the Motru region. This article highlights thick seam mining in the major coal and lignite mines in Romania, and surveys some improvements in mining technologies used at the coal face.

entry.dc:title: PRODUCTION RECORDS TUMBLE AT SISHEN IRON ORE MINE.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.prism:publicationName: South African Mining and Engineering Journal
entry.dc:description: Iscor's opencast mining operation has been producing high grade iron ore since 1953, but real growth has only come in the past seven years. Production has increased steadily and in the past few months tonnage records have been broken.

entry.dc:title: OPENCAST COAL IN BURGUNDY.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Extraction of coal by surface mining in France, while not extensive, is nevertheless of growing interest. Environmental considerations are of prime importance, particularly when operations are conducted close to towns and other industry. Rehabilitation may be required to improve the site for the benefit of the local community. This article surveys equipment and techniques used in opencast mining of coal at Montceau-les-Mines, Burgundy, France.
